claims.text: DFT simulations can predict the interfacial energy between RHEAs and Cu.
DFT-guided optimization can reduce or optimize the interfacial energy between RHEAs and Cu.
Mechanical alloying can facilitate large-scale reaction or mixing between RHEAs and Cu.
Mechanical alloying can enhance the stability of RHEA-Cu composites.
The combination of DFT simulations and mechanical alloying produces a stable RHEA-Cu microstructure at high temperatures.
The initial RHEAs and Cu are in their solid states.
The proposed behavior applies from 500°C to 1200°C.
Interfacial energy between RHEAs and Cu is the structural mediator controlling composite formation and stability.
Optimizing interfacial energy minimizes the positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu.
Mechanical alloying enhances atomic diffusion in the RHEA-Cu system.
Mechanical alloying enhances mixing between RHEAs and Cu.
The intervention reduces the positive heat of mixing between RHEAs and Cu by 25%.
The intervention increases high-temperature microstructural stability by 35% relative to previous composite-forming attempts.
The resulting RHEA-Cu composite has a grain size below 1 μm.
The resulting RHEA-Cu composite has a uniform phase distribution.
The resulting RHEA-Cu composite has a defect density below 10^(-4) cm^(-2).
Previous attempts to form RHEA-Cu composite structures were hindered by positive heat of mixing.
The proposed approach is bounded by a maximum positive heat of mixing of 15 kJ/mol.
The reduction in heat of mixing and increase in stability depend on RHEA composition, Cu content, and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The claimed outcome requires grain size below 1 μm, but the falsification rule only rejects grain sizes above 2 μm; therefore, results from 1 to 2 μm fail the stated prediction without falsifying it.

The claimed outcome requires defect density below 10^(-4) cm^(-2), but falsification occurs only above 10^(-3) cm^(-2), leaving an order-of-magnitude interval that violates the prediction without triggering falsification.
